## Beyond the Research Paper

Not every interesting question becomes a research project. This page is where I keep shorter observations, ideas, and questions that develop through my coursework, reading, and interest in international affairs.

My academic work has made me increasingly interested in how large global changes are experienced at the level of individual states. Economic transitions, geopolitical competition, migration, changing patterns of trade, and new technologies may be global developments, but governments respond to them in very different ways.

For me, the Middle East and Gulf provide an especially interesting setting for thinking about these questions. States such as Kuwait are navigating economic diversification while also responding to changes in energy markets, regional politics, technology, and the wider global economy.

## Questions I'm Thinking About

Some of the questions that currently interest me include:

- What does successful economic diversification actually look like for Gulf states?
- How much can governments reshape economies that have developed around natural-resource revenues?
- How do geopolitical changes affect the economic choices available to smaller states?
- What role will technology and data play in the future of government and political decision-making?
- How can quantitative evidence improve the way we understand political questions without losing their historical and regional context?

These questions do not always have simple answers. They are areas I hope to continue exploring as my academic interests develop.

## From Data to Politics

Studying data analysis alongside International Relations has also changed the way I approach political questions.

Political arguments often involve broad claims about countries, institutions, economies, and societies. Working with quantitative methods has encouraged me to ask what evidence supports those claims, how concepts can be measured, and what conclusions the available data actually allow us to make.

At the same time, numbers alone cannot explain every political outcome. Understanding history, institutions, geography, and political context remains essential. I am interested in the space between these approaches and in learning how they can complement one another.

## Looking Ahead

As I continue my undergraduate studies, I want this page to develop alongside my interests. Some notes may begin with something discussed in class, others with a political or economic development that catches my attention, and others with a question raised while working with data.

The purpose is not to provide a finished answer every time. It is to document the questions worth thinking about and how my understanding of them changes over time.
